15 / The learning salon

Fact or myth?

A historical fog detector. Five claims, verifiable sources and a clear distinction between Ada’s words and our jokes.

?!

Make a guess before revealing the explanation. In history, the most honest answer is sometimes “needs context”.

01

Ada was the first programmer.

Reveal the explanation and source

Needs context

She is often described this way in connection with the procedure published in 1843. Her collaboration with Babbage and the originality of individual contributions remain subjects of historical discussion. The title is shorthand, not the whole story.

Computer History Museum ↗
02

She only translated someone else’s article.

Reveal the explanation and source

Myth

She added extensive notes to Menabrea’s article, including a computational procedure. Her published contribution therefore went beyond translation alone.

Computer History Museum ↗
03

She ran her program on a completed Analytical Engine.

Reveal the explanation and source

Myth

The Analytical Engine was not completed during her lifetime. The table in Note G described planned operations, not a record of a successful run on a finished machine.

Computer History Museum ↗
04

She also considered machine-generated music.

Reveal the explanation and source

Fact

She imagined manipulating symbols beyond ordinary arithmetic, provided their relationships could be expressed as rules. Note A mentions the possibility of composing music.

Note G, 1843 ↗
05

Her B7 is today’s seventh Bernoulli number.

Reveal the explanation and source

Myth

Historical B7 in Note G corresponds to modern B8 = -1/30. Modern B7 is zero. Always check the notation when reading old formulas.

Note G, 1843 ↗
Verified historical quotation

What Ada actually wrote

“The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate any thing.”

Original English wording, retaining the historical spelling “any thing”.

Note G, 1843. She is discussing the Analytical Engine and the instructions we can give it. This quotation alone does not settle debates about modern AI’s capabilities.

Note G, 1843 ↗
A fictional line for this website

What our salon puts in her mouth

Tea first, compiler second.

We made up this sentence for fun. It is not a historical Ada Lovelace quotation. Her modern startups and beach coding are fictional too.
